title: Linear Inequalities, Part 2: Medium and Hard Problems

beats.say: In part one, we solved an inequality like an equation, and we flipped the sign when we divided by a negative number.

card.text: Divide by a negative: flip the sign

beats.say: In this video, we solve a word problem that needs rounding, a compound inequality, and then a hard problem with a system of inequalities.
Medium example one. A car rental costs forty dollars plus sixty-five cents per mile. The budget is at most one hundred twenty dollars. What's the greatest whole number of miles that fits the budget?
At most means less than or equal to. The fee is a constant, and the cost per mile multiplies m, so the inequality is forty plus zero point six five m is at most one hundred twenty.
Subtract forty from both sides. One hundred twenty minus forty is eighty.
Divide both sides by zero point six five. Eighty divided by zero point six five is about one hundred twenty-three point zero seven. The sign stays the same, because we divided by a positive number.
The question asks for the greatest whole number of miles. Since m must be at most one hundred twenty-three point zero seven, we round down. One hundred twenty-four miles would cost too much.
Medium example two. Solve the compound inequality negative five is less than one minus three x, which is at most ten. We do each step to all three parts.
The x term is in the middle, so we work on all three parts at once, doing the same step to each.
Subtract one from all three parts. Negative five minus one is negative six, and ten minus one is nine.
Divide all three parts by negative three. This flips both signs. Negative six divided by negative three is two, and nine divided by negative three is negative three.
Read the result from the smaller number up. x is at least negative three, and less than two.

Hard example. The point a comma four is a solution to the system y is at least x minus three, and y is less than negative two x plus sixteen. If a is an integer, what's the greatest possible value of a?

card.sub: (a, 4) is a solution. Greatest integer a?

beats.say: The point must satisfy both inequalities. So we substitute y equals four into each one, solve for a, and then keep only the values that satisfy both.
Substitute y equals four into the first inequality, to get four is at least a minus three.
Add three to both sides. Four plus three is seven. So seven is at least a, which means a is at most seven.
Written with a first, that says a is less than or equal to seven, which is our first condition on a.
Now substitute y equals four into the second inequality. We get four is less than negative two a plus sixteen.
Subtract sixteen from both sides, to move the plain number away from the x term. Four minus sixteen is negative twelve.
Divide both sides by negative two, and flip the sign. Negative twelve divided by negative two is six, so six is greater than a.
Written with a first, that says a is less than six, which is our second condition on a.
Both conditions must hold. a must be at most seven, and a must be less than six. The stricter condition wins, so a is less than six. The greatest integer less than six is five.

scenes.title: Check a equals five and six

beats.say: Check a equals five. In the first inequality, four is at least two, which is true, and in the second, four is less than six, which is true. Now check a equals six. Four is less than four is false, so six doesn't work.
To recap. In context problems, round down for the greatest whole number, and round up for the least whole number.
beats.item: Greatest rounds down, least rounds up

beats.say: In a compound inequality, do every step to all three parts, and flip both signs when you divide by a negative.
beats.item: Compound: all three parts, flip both signs

beats.say: For a system, substitute and solve each inequality, then keep what satisfies both. In the next video, we look at common traps and the fast way with Desmos.
